name: The Borrowdale Yews (the Fraternal Four)
age_estimate: roughly 1,500 years for the oldest of the three surviving trees

location.address: Hillside above Seathwaite, near Borrowdale, Cumbria, England (National Trust land)

access: Free. National Trust land, reached on foot: cross the bridge over the River Derwent near Seathwaite, then follow rough tracks and a footpath about half a mile up the hillside (not a paved or fully level path).
transport: No public transport reaches Seathwaite directly; nearest railway is Penrith or Windermere, then bus/car to Borrowdale/Seathwaite and the half-mile walk above. Exact stop and walk time not independently confirmed this pass.
verify_notes: ENSEMBLE entry, one collectible point (compact famous grove, one obvious place to stand): William Wordsworth's 'Fraternal Four' from his 1803-inspired poem 'Yew Trees' ('those fraternal Four of Borrowdale, / Joined in one solemn and capacious grove'), widely called the most famous yews in England. Only THREE of the original four survive; the fourth fell at an unrecorded date and is described as of unknown sex. Despite Wordsworth's 'Four' implying male trees, at least three of the surviving/fallen trees are female. Girths per Ancient Yew Group (June 2002 Tim Hills survey): largest 752-756cm (two sources round slightly differently, both cited), second 506cm, third 447cm, fourth (the Lorton/riverbank yew sometimes counted as a fifth/bonus tree, not part of the historic Four) 330cm and in notably better health than its neighbours up the hill. AGE: the largest and oldest tree's age was established by dendrochronology at roughly 1,500 years per Forestry Journal (2026); used as age_min/max for the ensemble's oldest member, the other two are presumably younger but undated. DAMAGE, recorded rather than smoothed over: the largest tree was hit by storms in 1998 and again in January 2005 (crown reduced), is now hollow and growing back from partial live sections, and Forestry Journal reports visitors have lit fires inside its hollow trunk, causing further damage; still alive and regrowing canopy as of the 2026 visit report, not dead. The 2002 Great British Trees plaque at the site was noted by one visiting arborist-journalist as possibly standing by the wrong tree; recorded as an open discrepancy, not resolved. Owned/managed by National Trust, which has fenced the trees against livestock and deliberately avoids sentimental intervention beyond that. Pin: coordinates are the Ancient Yew Group's own map point for the ensemble (grove-level, not per-trunk), consistent with the lead's independently-sourced coordinate about 500m away; approximate because the grove spans some distance up a hillside and a visitor still has to locate each trunk once there.
